questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the defining feature of a democratic regime
questions.stem: While drafting the governance section of a design brief, Aiko argues that a regime counts as democratic only when voters can remove bad rulers.

options.text: Rulers may be replaced through regular, peaceful means and losers accept the result.
A codified constitution with entrenched rights is enough to settle the question.
options.misconception: believes a written constitution alone settles democracy

options.text: Sustained high voter turnout at every election is the decisive marker of democracy.
options.misconception: treats turnout levels as proof of democratic quality

options.text: Several competing parties guarantee that electoral outcomes will be truly accountable.
options.misconception: assumes many parties guarantee real accountability

questions.explanation: A democratic regime lets citizens remove rulers by regular, peaceful means and losers accept the result. Constitutions, turnout figures and party counts are only indicators, and none of them settles the question alone.
questions.hint: Focus on how rulers leave office.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish authoritarian rule from competitive politics

stimulus.body: The design brief records that the ruling group keeps a monopoly on the levers of coercion, while elections are held but opposition candidates are detained before polling day. Officials describe the polls as an affirmation of national unity rather than a contest. The brief adds that no candidate has ever won a seat against the ruling group.

questions.stem: Reading this excerpt from the brief, which characterisation of the regime described in it fits best?

options.text: A democratic regime in which voters freely choose among rival programmes.
options.misconception: assumes elections alone make a regime democratic

options.text: An authoritarian regime that uses elections to legitimate rule without real competition.
A hybrid regime in which power alternates freely between two rival blocs.
options.misconception: mistakes controlled polls for genuine alternation

options.text: A transitional regime preparing free and fair polls in the next electoral cycle.
options.misconception: reads every poll as a step toward free elections

questions.explanation: Detaining opposition candidates and monopolising coercion removes real competition, so the polls are managed. Elections that no incumbent can lose legitimise authoritarian rule rather than reveal it.
questions.hint: Ask whether an incumbent could actually lose.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the plurality rule to a divided district
questions.stem: In the design brief, Nadia must model a district where three candidates split the vote thirty-four, thirty-three and thirty-three percent.

options.text: The seat stays vacant until one candidate reaches fifty percent of the vote.
options.misconception: assumes a majority threshold always applies

options.text: The seat goes to the candidate backed by the largest organised party membership.
options.misconception: confuses votes cast with party membership size

options.text: The candidate with the most votes wins the seat without needing a majority.
The seat is decided by a runoff between the two leading candidates.
options.misconception: assumes a second round is always required

questions.explanation: Plurality awards the seat to the largest vote share even without a majority, so a three-way split produces a weak winner. Runoffs and membership counts belong to other rules and do not apply here.
questions.hint: Check the rule for a split vote.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why proportional systems use thresholds and remainders
questions.stem: In the design brief, Nadia must explain to the client why a proportional system is usually paired with a legal threshold.

answer.exemplar: A threshold exists because a pure proportional system would award seats to every party with only a sliver of the national vote, producing a fragmented chamber and unstable governments. Excluding very small parties under a legal floor preserves the proportional relationship between votes and seats while keeping the number of viable parties manageable, which is why thresholds and proportional allocation travel together in most systems that use them.

questions.explanation: Proportional allocation mirrors vote shares, so without a floor every tiny party gains seats. The threshold filters the tail while leaving the proportional logic intact.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to tiny parties.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Classify a state by the protection of subunit powers
questions.stem: In the design brief, Tomas notes that two regional units keep their own rulebooks, the centre legislates in listed fields, and the highest court settles disputes between them.

options.text: A federal system in which regional units hold powers the centre cannot unilaterally reclaim.
A unitary system in which the centre may redirect regional powers at any time.
options.misconception: treats regional autonomy as revocable by the centre

options.text: A confederation in which the centre has no law-making role of its own.
options.misconception: mistakes a written constitution for a loose confederation

options.text: A hybrid regime where regional autonomy rests on party discipline.
options.misconception: confuses institutional structure with regime type

questions.explanation: Constitutionally protected regional powers that the centre cannot simply reclaim mark a federal arrangement. In a unitary state those powers stay legally subordinate to the centre, whatever practice looks like.
questions.hint: Ask who can legally reclaim regional powers.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Contrast unitary and federal allocation of authority
questions.stem: Mira's design brief states that one national legislature sets rules for the whole territory and that local authorities exist only as bodies created by central statute.

options.text: A federal system, since local bodies are written into the constitution.
options.misconception: assumes any local body implies constitutional federalism

options.text: A unitary system in which all authority ultimately rests with the national centre.
A hybrid regime where local bodies act as political parties.
options.misconception: confuses administrative structure with regime classification

options.text: A confederal state with a weak central parliament.
options.misconception: treats a strong centre as a confederal arrangement

questions.explanation: Unitary states place all legal authority in the centre, which may create or abolish local bodies as it wishes. Federalism requires subunits to hold protected rights, so their mere existence proves nothing.
questions.hint: Check whether local powers can be withdrawn.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Separate parliamentary and presidential executive design

stimulus.body: The governance module notes that a head of state appoints a prime minister who must hold the confidence of the legislature. A vote of no confidence removes the cabinet, and a successor must again seek legislative support. The brief records that the head of state has no policy authority in this arrangement.

questions.stem: Reading this passage from the brief, which description of the executive design fits best?

options.text: A presidential system where the executive answers to the legislature.
options.misconception: reverses the accountability direction between branches

options.text: A hybrid regime in which no branch can remove the others.
options.misconception: assumes mutual independence rules out confidence politics

options.text: A parliamentary system where the government depends on legislative confidence.
A unitary system in which the head of state holds sole authority.
options.misconception: reads a ceremonial presidency as unitary rule

questions.explanation: A government that survives only while the legislature supports it defines the parliamentary design. A presidential executive holds a separate mandate and cannot be removed by a no-confidence vote.
questions.hint: Check who can dismiss the government.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the features of a hybrid regime
questions.stem: In a later brief the author insists a regime can hold regular elections, ban the strongest opposition party, and still carry the label hybrid rather than authoritarian.

options.text: Because elections are held regularly, the regime is plainly democratic.
options.misconception: treats regular elections as sufficient for democracy

options.text: Because the opposition is banned, the regime must be fully authoritarian.
options.misconception: conflates one unfair practice with total authoritarianism

options.text: Because labels are contested, no regime type can be assigned at all.
options.misconception: denies classification because categories are debated

options.text: Because competitive elections coexist with serious unfairness and weak accountability.

questions.explanation: Hybrid regimes combine electoral competition with serious distortions such as bans on rivals. Regular polls alone do not clear a regime of authoritarianism, and one unfair practice does not make it wholly authoritarian.
questions.hint: Look for competition combined with unfairness.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a proportional seat table correctly
questions.stem: In the brief, Mira must explain to a client how to read a proportional seat table that gives a party more seats than its vote share.

answer.exemplar: A seat total exceeding the party's vote share is normal under proportional allocation, because seats are assigned to fill the chamber after votes are converted into whole members. The surplus arises from remainders and rounding, not from over-representation in the sense of a deliberate bias, so the correct reading is that the party held its proportional entitlement and the small gap reflects the impossibility of dividing a fixed number of seats into exact fractional shares.

questions.explanation: Seats must be whole numbers, so remainders and rounding decide who gains the surplus. The result stays within the proportional entitlement rather than signalling a deliberate tilt.
questions.hint: Remember seats cannot be fractional.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish devolution from delegation and federalism
questions.stem: The design brief proposes that a national statute delegate parking enforcement to a city council that national law can withdraw at any time.

options.text: This is devolution, because a subunit now performs a national function.
options.misconception: confuses shared administration with transferred sovereignty

options.text: This is delegation, because the centre keeps legal authority and can reclaim it.
This is federalism, because authority is divided between two levels of government.
options.misconception: assumes any division of work implies constitutional federalism

options.text: This is nothing at all, since no new body was created by the delegation.
options.misconception: believes delegation requires creating a new institution

questions.explanation: Delegation lends tasks to another body while the centre keeps the right to reclaim them. Devolution and federalism both involve powers the centre cannot simply reclaim at will.
questions.hint: Ask who keeps the power to withdraw.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the defining feature of a democratic regime
questions.stem: Later, Felix drafts a note claiming that a regime is democratic whenever elections are contested by more than one candidate.

options.text: Only regimes where the opposition can actually win count as democratic.
options.misconception: treats opposition victory odds as the measure of democracy

options.text: Any regime holding elections on a fixed cycle qualifies as democratic.
options.misconception: confuses a regular electoral calendar with real competition

options.text: A regime is democratic when power can change hands without force.
A regime is democratic when the constitution names specific rights.
options.misconception: believes written rights alone make a regime democratic

questions.explanation: The core of democracy is that rulers can be replaced and they accept the result. Multiple candidates or a fixed electoral calendar may be necessary but neither alone guarantees change.
questions.hint: Ask whether the winner can actually lose.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish authoritarian rule from competitive politics

stimulus.body: The review notes that the legislature is stacked in favour of the ruling party and that the courts have been reshuffled since the last dispute. Critical broadcasters have lost their licences, although a handful of local council seats were contested and some were won by opponents. Officials describe the recent local results as a sign of healthy local participation.

questions.stem: Judging from this description in the brief, what best captures the regime described?

options.text: A fully democratic regime, since some local offices remain contested.
options.misconception: mistakes token local contests for national democracy

options.text: A hybrid regime in which national competition is entirely intact.
options.misconception: ignores the stacked courts and closed media

options.text: A unitary system, since central control reaches down to local councils.
options.misconception: confuses centralisation of power with unitary state structure

options.text: An authoritarian regime whose local contests are permitted but not meaningful.

questions.explanation: Authoritarian regimes often allow token local contests to project normality while the institutions that matter are stacked. A contest that cannot affect who governs proves nothing about democracy.
questions.hint: Ask whether local results affect who governs.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the plurality rule to a divided district
questions.stem: Sara contrasts two districts, one where the top candidate won forty percent and another where the top candidate won thirty-five percent.

options.text: Both winners took office under plurality, with the larger share in the first district.
Only the first winner qualifies, since a majority threshold is required.
options.misconception: applies a majority threshold to a plurality rule

options.text: Neither winner qualifies, because forty percent is a minority of the total.
options.misconception: requires a majority even though the rule is plurality

options.text: The second district required a runoff, while the first did not.
options.misconception: invents a runoff rule that the brief never states

questions.explanation: Plurality ignores whether the winner has a majority, so both seats are filled by the top vote-getter. The difference between forty and thirty-five percent is the size of the win, not its validity.
questions.hint: Compare the rule, not the margin.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why proportional systems use thresholds and remainders
questions.stem: Sara must explain in the brief why proportional systems often look fairer for minority parties than plurality districts.

answer.exemplar: Proportional allocation ties seats to the overall vote share across the whole country, so a party that wins twelve percent of the vote can expect roughly twelve percent of seats, whereas a plurality district system can leave that party with no seats at all if its support is spread thinly across constituencies. The trade-off is that geographic concentration of support can deliver a party far more seats under plurality than its national vote share would suggest, so fairness for dispersed minorities is the advantage proportional systems are designed to deliver.

questions.explanation: Proportional rules tie seats to national vote shares, so dispersed minorities are not erased by district boundaries. Plurality can ignore a party's votes entirely when its support is scattered.
questions.hint: Compare how votes convert to seats.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Classify a state by the protection of subunit powers
questions.stem: A second brief describes a state where the constitution lists exclusive powers for each level and both levels may tax and legislate independently.

options.text: A unitary state, since all legislation ultimately serves one national interest.
options.misconception: assumes constitutional guarantees imply central supremacy

options.text: A federal state where each level holds constitutionally guaranteed powers.
A confederation, because the units are legally equal and independent.
options.misconception: mistakes equal division for a loose confederation

options.text: A hybrid regime, because the constitution divides political competition.
options.misconception: confuses state structure with democratic regime type

questions.explanation: Two levels holding constitutionally guaranteed legislative powers make the arrangement federal. Confederation implies a much looser centre with no independent legislative role, and regime type is a separate question.
questions.hint: Check whether both levels legislate independently.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Contrast unitary and federal allocation of authority
questions.stem: The brief notes that one parliament may pass a law binding the whole territory, and a central ministry may create or abolish any regional office it dislikes.

options.text: A federal state, because the ministry must also respect regional charters.
options.misconception: presumes a constitutional limit on central abolition

options.text: A confederation, because regional offices are organised around distinct identities.
options.misconception: confuses local administration with a confederation

options.text: A unitary state, since the centre creates and abolishes regional bodies freely.
A hybrid regime, because local offices compete with central authority.
options.misconception: reads administrative hierarchy as regime hybridity

questions.explanation: The hallmark of a unitary state is that the centre can reorganise the territory and its bodies by ordinary law. Federalism would bar such central control over constitutionally protected units.
questions.hint: Test whether the centre can undo local bodies.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Separate parliamentary and presidential executive design

stimulus.body: The client describes a country where a directly elected president serves a fixed five-year term and cannot be dismissed by the legislature. At the same time a prime minister heads the government and must hold the confidence of the chamber to stay in office. The note adds that early dissolution of the chamber is constitutionally barred.

questions.stem: Which description of the executive design matches the arrangement described in the brief?

options.text: A presidential element within a parliamentary system of government.
A purely parliamentary system where the head of state is symbolic.
options.misconception: assumes a fixed term rules out parliamentary features

options.text: A purely presidential system where the prime minister answers to the legislature.
options.misconception: reverses which office answers to the legislature

options.text: A hybrid regime where no branch holds a separate mandate.
options.misconception: treats any dual executive as evidence of hybridity

questions.explanation: A fixed-term directly elected president is a presidential element, and a confidence-dependent prime minister is a parliamentary one. Mixing executive designs does not make a regime hybrid, which describes electoral unfairness.
questions.hint: Separate executive design from electoral fairness.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the features of a hybrid regime
questions.stem: Another draft insists a regime with real but unfair elections should be labelled hybrid rather than either democracy or authoritarianism.

options.text: The label should be democracy, because some competition and some unfairness coexist.
options.misconception: assumes partial competition earns a democratic label

options.text: The label should be hybrid, because electoral competition is real yet systematically unfair.
The label should be authoritarian, because any unfairness cancels the competition.
options.misconception: treats unfairness as erasing all competition

options.text: The label should be hybrid, because hybrids sit halfway between the two extremes.
options.misconception: defines hybrids by position on a spectrum instead of practice

questions.explanation: Hybrid is right because competition is genuine while unfairness systematically distorts it. The label describes the quality of elections, not a midpoint between two extremes.
questions.hint: Judge the elections themselves.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a proportional seat table correctly
questions.stem: Omar must explain in the brief how to read a proportional table where three parties together hold a clear seat majority.

answer.exemplar: A seat majority for a bloc of parties does not by itself convert the system into a majoritarian one, because under proportional rules seats are distributed in proportion to votes and the arithmetic of rounding decides whether a bloc clears the halfway mark. The brief should tell the client to compare the bloc's seat total against the threshold for a majority and to check whether the underlying votes gave the bloc anything near half the vote, since seat majorities built on a third of the vote signal fragmented representation rather than a popular majority.

questions.explanation: Seat majorities can arise from proportional arithmetic when rounding tips coalitions over the halfway line. The client should compare the bloc's vote share with its seat share before drawing conclusions.
questions.hint: Compare seat share with vote share.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish devolution from delegation and federalism
questions.stem: The brief's legal section states that a settlement devolved to the regional assembly includes its own tax base and its own courts.

options.text: This is autonomy, since no national parliament retains any oversight role.
options.misconception: assumes devolution removes any national oversight

options.text: This is delegation, since the centre may withdraw the powers by statute.
options.misconception: assumes all regional power stays recoverable by the centre

options.text: This is federalism, since two units now legislate on the same subjects.
options.misconception: equates devolution with constitutional division of powers

options.text: This is devolution, since the assembly holds powers the centre has surrendered.

questions.explanation: Devolution transfers powers that the centre gives up and does not simply reclaim at will; tax and courts are classic examples. Federalism is a constitutional division between levels, while delegation leaves the centre's legal grip intact.
questions.hint: Test whether the centre can reclaim it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the defining feature of a democratic regime
questions.stem: Lena's civic technology brief says the platform will only count a state as democratic when votes can be contested and counted honestly.

options.text: A written constitution guarantees democracy even where counting is rigged.
options.misconception: believes constitutional text overrides electoral practice

options.text: The presence of a parliament is sufficient to classify the state as democratic.
options.misconception: treats the mere existence of a legislature as sufficient

options.text: Free association alone shows a state is democratic without any electoral test.
options.misconception: ignores whether votes can be contested at all

options.text: Competition and honest counting together define the democratic minimum here.

questions.explanation: The brief's test has two parts, genuine competition and honest counting, and both must hold. A parliament, free association or a constitution is evidence at best, since any can coexist with rigged ballots.
questions.hint: Apply both parts of the stated test.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish authoritarian rule from competitive politics

stimulus.body: The design review records that the ruling party appoints every member of the electoral commission. Applications to hold opposition rallies are routinely refused on technical grounds, and the surviving newspapers carry only official statements. Officials defend the arrangement as a way of preventing disorder during a difficult transition.

questions.stem: Which description best fits the regime presented in this design review extract?

options.text: A democratic regime with unusually strict rules on public assembly.
options.misconception: reads repression of assembly as ordinary legal restriction

options.text: An authoritarian regime where competition is obstructed at every stage.
A hybrid regime with meaningful competition but administrative bias.
options.misconception: treats systematic obstruction as mere administrative bias

options.text: A unitary state whose administrative rules apply only to rallies.
options.misconception: confuses a regime type with a state structure

questions.explanation: Control of the electoral commission, refused permits and a scripted press show competition removed rather than tilted. Systematic obstruction of this kind is the hallmark of authoritarian rule.
questions.hint: Weigh the obstacles added together.

questions.stem: In another module Priya compares a four-way district where the leader takes twenty-eight percent with a two-way district.

options.text: The four-way district needs a runoff, since no candidate reached a majority.
options.misconception: introduces a runoff requirement the rule does not contain

options.text: The two-way district is invalid, since a majority is required to win.
options.misconception: applies a majority rule to a two-candidate contest

options.text: The four-way district should be redrawn before any seat is awarded.
options.misconception: treats redrawing as the remedy for a low winning share

options.text: Both seats go to the highest vote-getter under the same plurality rule.

questions.explanation: Plurality is indifferent to whether the winner has a majority, so the same rule covers both districts and the leader takes the seat in each. Runoffs and redrawing are not part of the rule described.
questions.hint: Same rule, different margins.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why proportional systems use thresholds and remainders
questions.stem: Priya must justify in the design brief why proportional allocation is chosen over single-member districts for the regional council.

answer.exemplar: The brief should argue that proportional allocation is preferred when the council must represent the whole electorate rather than a set of geographic strongholds. Under single-member districts a party with a well-organised but geographically narrow support base can win few or no seats despite a substantial national vote, while proportional allocation converts national votes into seats directly, so regional minorities and new parties gain representation without abandoning constituency service. The client should be told that this comes at the cost of weaker personal accountability to a district, which is the trade the council must weigh.

questions.explanation: Proportional rules tie seats to the national vote so that dispersed support is not wiped out by district lines. The client buys that inclusiveness at the cost of weaker local accountability.
questions.hint: Think about what seat conversion buys.

questions.stem: Based on the arrangement described in the brief, which executive design is in operation?

options.text: A presidential system with a ceremonial head of state and an elected government.
options.misconception: assumes an elected government implies a presidential design

options.text: A hybrid regime where the head of state holds real governing powers.
options.misconception: invents governing powers for a ceremonial head of state

options.text: A parliamentary system where the government rests on legislative confidence.

options.misconception: treats a unicameral legislature as a unitary state

questions.explanation: A government removable by no-confidence and formed by the majority party is the parliamentary design, with a ceremonial head of state. A presidential executive is elected directly and cannot be voted out by the legislature.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise the features of a hybrid regime
questions.stem: One reviewer argues that a regime with meaningful elections and real incumbents losing office is plain democracy, not hybrid.

options.text: The reviewer is right, because genuine alternation settles the classification.
options.misconception: assumes clean alternation rules out electoral unfairness

options.text: The reviewer is wrong, because hybrid regimes can also include real alternation.
The reviewer is right, because hybrid status requires the absence of competition.
options.misconception: believes hybrids must lack any real competition

options.text: The reviewer is wrong, because every imperfect democracy counts as hybrid.
options.misconception: widens the hybrid label to cover all imperfect systems

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a proportional seat table correctly
questions.stem: The design brief must teach staff how to explain a proportional table in which the largest party has thirty-eight percent of votes.

answer.exemplar: With thirty-eight percent of the vote the largest party is entitled to roughly thirty-eight percent of seats, and the remaining seats are shared among the other parties in the same proportion, so the table is a faithful mirror of the vote. The staff note should add two cautions: first, seat numbers are whole, so remainders are distributed and small parties gain or lose a seat, and second, a single bloc may still command a seat majority if the arithmetic of rounding favours it, which is why blocs and coalitions must be checked against the halfway line rather than assumed.

questions.explanation: A proportional table should mirror the vote split once rounding is allowed for. Staff must add that remainders shift seats and that bloc arithmetic can still deliver a majority.
questions.hint: Mirror the votes, then check rounding.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish devolution from delegation and federalism

stimulus.body: The summary describes a devolved body that sets its own service standards for local transport and publishes its own performance targets. Under the settlement the body must submit an annual report to the national legislature, and a ministerial committee may request further information. The centre retains control of the legislation that funds the service.

questions.stem: How does the arrangement described in the brief sit between delegation and devolution?

options.misconception: assumes any reporting rule reverts powers to the centre

options.text: It is devolution with oversight, since the powers are transferred and retained.
It is delegation, because the devolved body may set its own standards.
options.misconception: mistakes operational autonomy for transferred legal authority

options.text: It is federalism, because the devolved body reports to the national legislature.
options.misconception: confuses a reporting duty with constitutional division

questions.explanation: Setting service standards indicates transferred authority, and annual reporting is compatible with devolution. Devolution is not a constitutional split of sovereignty, and oversight does not undo a transfer.
questions.hint: Separate transfer of power from reporting duty.

options.misconception: reduces democracy to vote counting alone

options.text: This is too narrow, because only voting rights matter in a democracy.
options.misconception: assumes voting rights exhaust democratic standards

options.text: This captures electoral accountability, one part of a broader democratic test.
This is wrong, because recounts are a feature of aristocratic government.
options.misconception: claims recount rights belong to aristocratic government

questions.explanation: Contesting counts is a genuine democratic guarantee, but it covers electoral integrity rather than the whole picture. Democracy also needs real competition for office and freedom from coercion.

In the second the elections look competitive on paper, but the main opposition figure was sentenced to a long term and has not stood since.

questions.stem: Comparing the two cases in the extract, what is the most accurate generalisation about authoritarian rule?

options.text: Authoritarian rule is visible only where the press is controlled.
options.misconception: assumes press control is a necessary condition

options.text: Authoritarian rule requires the complete absence of competitive elections.
options.misconception: defines authoritarianism by absence of any elections

options.text: Authoritarian rule is best judged only by how often elections are held.
options.misconception: measures authoritarianism only by election frequency

options.text: Authoritarian rule can rest on emergency powers or on imprisoning rivals.

questions.explanation: Authoritarian rule takes many forms, from emergency powers suspending elections to jailing rivals while polls look competitive. What matters is whether rulers can be removed, not the calendar's cosmetics.

options.text: The thirty-one percent district was miscounted and needs a new poll.
options.misconception: treats a weak plurality as evidence of miscounting

options.misconception: believes plurality requires an outright majority

questions.explanation: Plurality asks only who received the most votes, so a winner with thirty-one percent is as valid as one with fifty-one percent. The margin affects how strong the mandate looks, not whether the result stands.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why proportional systems use thresholds and remainders
questions.stem: Tariq must write in the brief how a proportional result converts into the coalition arithmetic of government formation.

answer.exemplar: In a proportional system each party is first given seats in rough proportion to its vote, and only then does the arithmetic of government formation begin: no single party usually reaches a majority, so the largest party must find partners whose seats together exceed the halfway mark. The brief should explain that this search happens after the election, that it depends on the arithmetic of remainders and on the distribution of votes across parties, and that voters have no direct say in which parties end up governing together.

questions.explanation: Proportional allocation produces a fragmented chamber where majorities are assembled after the vote. Coalition building therefore depends on seat arithmetic rather than on a direct mandate.
questions.hint: Arithmetic comes after the vote.

options.misconception: reads a division of powers as evidence of electoral unfairness

options.misconception: treats a coordinating council as confederation status

options.misconception: assumes an elected presidency makes the prime minister subordinate

options.text: A hybrid regime because the two branches hold incompatible mandates.
options.misconception: confuses mixed executive mandates with electoral unfairness

options.text: A unitary state because only one level of government is described.
options.misconception: treats one institutional level as proof of a unitary state

options.text: The claim holds, because media bias is a matter of taste rather than law.
options.misconception: dismisses media bias as a matter of preference

options.misconception: sets an absolute standard beyond the hybrid category

questions.explanation: Competitive elections with systematic bias and harassment are the classic hybrid pattern, so the claim fails on unfairness, not on competition. Media bias is a matter of law and fact, not taste.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a proportional seat table correctly
questions.stem: Sora must explain in the brief why a proportional table can show a party with fewer votes than a rival holding more seats.

answer.exemplar: The brief should explain that proportional allocation works by dividing the available seats among parties in the light of their votes and then distributing the leftover seats as remainders, so tiny differences in vote share can be magnified by a favourable rounding decision in one district and an unfavourable one in another. A party can therefore finish with more seats even with marginally fewer votes, and this is a mechanical artefact of whole-number allocation rather than evidence of a deliberate bias in the electoral rules themselves.

questions.explanation: Whole-seat allocation and remainders mean near-equal vote shares can convert into different seat totals. The divergence is mechanical, not a deliberate tilt in the rules.
questions.hint: Rounding decides who gains the remainder.

options.misconception: treats a rare case as if it never occurred

options.misconception: equates normal elections with democratic accountability

options.text: An authoritarian regime where checks on removal protect incumbents indefinitely.
A hybrid regime, because the votes are competitive but the outcome is fixed.
options.misconception: applies the hybrid label to a system without real competition

options.text: A unitary state, because the assembly holds the decisive legal power.
options.misconception: confuses the location of legal power with the regime type

questions.explanation: Rules that make incumbents effectively irremovable place the system outside democracy even though votes are organised normally. The decisive feature is whether office can be lost, not whether a ballot was counted.

A proportional district, where seats are allocated across the whole country.

options.misconception: invents a second round that the briefing never mentions

options.misconception: confuses single-member with single transferable vote

questions.explanation: One seat per district decided by the largest vote share is single-member plurality. Proportional allocation works across the whole country, a second round must be specified, and transferable votes allow ranking.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why proportional systems use thresholds and remainders
questions.stem: Rosa must explain in the design brief how proportional seats differ from constituency results for a party with strong local support.

answer.exemplar: The brief should distinguish the two levels of result clearly: under a constituency rule a party can win a district outright on a small share of the national vote, and under proportional allocation its seats are determined by its share of the national vote as a whole. A party concentrated in one area may therefore look dominant in its district yet win few seats proportionally, while a party whose support is spread evenly gains seats in every region. The client should be told which figure matters for their purpose, because the two measures answer different questions about representation.

questions.explanation: Constituency results measure local strength and proportional seats measure national share. Concentrated support wins districts but few proportional seats.
questions.hint: District strength is not the same as national share.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a proportional seat table correctly
questions.stem: The brief must show new analysts how a proportional table translates votes into seats when the total seat count is fixed.

answer.exemplar: The brief should show the arithmetic in three steps: first, calculate each party's vote share as a percentage of votes cast; second, multiply that share by the total number of seats to get its exact entitlement; third, distribute the seats that cannot be divided evenly using a stated remainder rule. questions.explanation: Proportional conversion runs vote share, fractional entitlement, then remainder allocation. The remainder rule decides the last seats and is a political choice.
questions.hint: Work through shares, entitlements, remainders.

questions.learningObjective: Separate parliamentary and presidential executive design

stimulus.body: The specification states that the head of state appoints the prime minister, and that the appointee must secure a confidence vote before taking office. A failure of confidence triggers fresh elections. The paragraph also notes that the head of state has no power to dismiss a prime minister who still enjoys legislative support.

questions.stem: Which label fits the executive design set out in this part of the brief?

options.text: A presidential system, because the head of state makes the key appointment.
options.misconception: treats a formal appointment as the source of real power

options.text: A parliamentary system, because the government depends on legislative confidence.
A hybrid regime, because a head of state retains some appointment power.
options.misconception: calls routine appointment power a marker of hybridity

options.text: A unitary state, because all decisions pass through one chamber.
options.misconception: mistakes a single chamber for a unitary state structure

questions.explanation: Appointment by a head of state is normal in parliamentary systems; what matters is that the government survives only with legislative confidence. A hybrid label would need evidence of unfair elections.
questions.hint: Focus on the confidence relationship.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the features of a hybrid regime
questions.stem: The last reviewer argues that a regime with regular polls, serious media bias and frequent disqualifications should be called authoritarian.

options.text: The label should be authoritarian, because disqualifications remove genuine competition.
options.misconception: collapses hybrid into authoritarian at the first unfair practice

options.text: The label should be democratic, because regular polls are held on schedule.
options.misconception: accepts a regular calendar as proof of a fair contest

options.text: The label should be hybrid, because competition survives alongside serious unfairness.
The label should be hybrid, because hybrids sit between the two ideal types.
options.misconception: defines the category by midpoint position instead of evidence

questions.explanation: Where polls stay competitive but bias and disqualifications are routine, the hybrid label fits: more than one unfair practice, yet not full authoritarianism. The category is defined by practice, not midpoint.
questions.hint: Weigh the whole pattern of unfairness.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a proportional seat table correctly
questions.stem: The closing annex asks students to explain why a proportional table alone does not reveal how governments will be formed.

answer.exemplar: The annex should make clear that a proportional table reports seats, not alliances. It shows what each party won on the vote and how those votes converted into members, but the table says nothing about which parties will talk to each other, whether a single party is one seat short of a majority, or whether the arithmetic of remainders makes a particular coalition the only viable route. Forming a government is a negotiation between parties after the count, and the annex should note that voters may never have expressed a preference for the combination that emerges.

questions.explanation: A seat table records votes and seats, not post-vote bargains. Coalition formation depends on negotiations and on how close the arithmetic leaves each party.
questions.hint: Seats are not alliances.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish devolution from delegation and federalism

stimulus.body: The summary states that the devolved legislature may enact its own laws on the subjects listed in the settlement. It also states that the national parliament may override those laws by a two-thirds majority. Officials describe the override as a last-resort safeguard rather than a routine instrument.

questions.stem: How should the arrangement described in the brief be characterised?

options.text: It is delegation, because the centre retains a veto over devolved laws.
options.misconception: equates a legislative veto with absence of transferred power

options.text: It is federalism, because two legislatures share law-making power.
options.misconception: mistakes a revocable grant for a constitutional division

options.text: It is devolution without limit, because the devolved body legislates freely.
options.misconception: ignores the override clause in the arrangement described

options.text: It is devolution with a legal limit, since the centre can override.

questions.explanation: A devolved legislature making its own laws is genuine devolution, and a centre override limits it rather than making it delegation. A revocable grant of law-making power is not a constitutional division of sovereignty.
questions.hint: A limit on devolution is still devolution.
